title: Energy, heat and temperature
html:
Guiding question

How can we measure the energy transferred during reactions?

Every reaction you have ever watched gives itself away somehow: a colour change, a gas fizzing off, a precipitate forming, or a temperature change. This topic is about the last of these. Energy is always transferred when bonds are broken and made, and much of chemistry (fuels, hand-warmers, cold packs, metabolism, industrial reactors) depends on knowing how much energy goes in or out.

R1.1.1 Energy transfer, system and surroundings

In a chemical reaction the total energy is conserved: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred. Chemical potential energy is stored in the bonds of the reactants and products. When the products store less chemical energy than the reactants, the difference is transferred out, usually as heat; when they store more, energy must be taken in.

To keep track of the energy we split the universe into two parts. The system is the reaction mixture (the reactants and products we are studying); everything else, including the water, the beaker, the thermometer and the air, is the surroundings.

  • Open system: matter and energy can cross the boundary (an open beaker: gases can escape and heat can leave).
  • Closed system: energy can cross, matter cannot (a sealed flask).
  • Isolated system: neither matter nor energy can cross (an ideal, perfectly insulated vacuum flask; it does not exist perfectly in practice).

A reaction is carried out in a stoppered conical flask that is not insulated. What type of system is this?

  1. Open
  2. Closed
  3. Isolated
  4. Adiabatic and open

The stopper stops matter escaping, but heat can still pass through the glass, so it is a closed system. An isolated system would need perfect insulation as well.

Heat is not the same as temperature

Temperature is a state function proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles. Heat (q) is energy transferred from a warmer body to a cooler one because of a temperature gradient. Use the two words precisely: heat is transferred; temperature is measured.

Think about a cup of water at 100 °C and a bucket of water at 50 °C. The particles in the cup move faster on average (higher temperature), but the bucket contains far more particles, so its total thermal energy store can be larger, and it would do a much better job of warming a swimming pool.

Key pointThe class analogy: imagine a room full of people. The money each person holds is like the temperature (the average energy per particle). The number of people is the number of particles. The total money in the room is the thermal energy store. A few rich people can hold less money in total than a large crowd of people who each have a little.

Which has more thermal energy: a bath of water at 40 °C or a cup of tea at 80 °C?

  1. The cup of tea, because its temperature is higher
  2. The bath, because it contains many more particles
  3. They are equal, because both are liquids
  4. It cannot be compared without knowing c

Temperature is the average kinetic energy per particle; thermal energy is the total. The bath has a lower average but vastly more particles, so its total is larger.

What happens to particles when they are heated?

A bar of Dove soap floats because it contains tiny pockets of air trapped during manufacture. Microwave it and the bar swells into a huge foamy cloud. The air particles in each pocket gain kinetic energy, move faster and collide harder and more often with the walls, so the pockets expand and stretch the softened soap.

The lesson from the demonstration: individual molecules do not "get hotter". When a substance is heated, its particles move or vibrate faster (more kinetic energy) and spread out. Temperature is a property of a large collection of particles, not of one molecule.

Exam tipWhich has the larger thermal energy store: an iceberg at −5 °C or a red-hot iron nail? The 4-mark answer: (1) the iceberg has a lower temperature; (2) but it contains vastly more particles; (3) so the total energy of all its vibrating particles is greater; (4) therefore the iceberg has the larger thermal energy store.
Predict first: write your own 4-mark answer to the iceberg question, then reveal a model answer

"Although the iron nail is at a much higher temperature, so its particles have a higher average kinetic energy, the iceberg contains an enormously larger number of particles. The thermal energy store is the total energy of all the particles, so the iceberg, with so many more vibrating particles, has the larger thermal energy store."

At constant pressure, the heat transferred between a closed system and its surroundings during a reaction is called the enthalpy change, ΔH, usually given in kJ (or kJ mol−1 once divided by the amount of reaction). You will meet ΔH properly in R1.1.4.

title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
html:
R1.1.2 Exothermic and endothermic reactions

Watch a match being struck, or the classic "cannon fire" demonstration, and the energy given out is obvious. Mix solid barium hydroxide octahydrate with ammonium thiocyanate (or ammonium chloride) in a beaker standing on a wet wooden block, and the beaker gets so cold that it freezes to the block. These two experiences define the two types of reaction.

DefinitionExothermic: heat is transferred from the system to the surroundings. The temperature of the surroundings rises and ΔH is negative.
Endothermic: heat is absorbed by the system from the surroundings. The mixture feels cold and ΔH is positive.

The word parts help: therm means heat (thermometer, thermostat), exo means out and endo means in. Dissolving NH4NO3 in water is the standard textbook example of an endothermic process; cold packs work this way.

The sign is always given from the point of view of the system. In an exothermic reaction the system loses enthalpy, so ΔH is negative even though the thermometer reading goes up. In an exothermic reaction the reactants give out heat to the surroundings; in an endothermic reaction the chemicals take in heat from their surroundings.

Why? Bond breaking and bond making

Every reaction involves breaking some bonds in the reactants and making new bonds in the products.

  • Breaking bonds absorbs energy (endothermic): energy is needed to pull atoms apart against their attraction.
  • Making bonds releases energy (exothermic): energy is given out as atoms are pulled together into a more stable arrangement.

The overall sign of ΔH depends on which of these is larger. If more energy is released making the new bonds than was absorbed breaking the old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall. If breaking the old bonds needs more energy than is released by making the new ones, it is endothermic.

Common mistakeA popular classroom shortcut is "exothermic = making bonds, endothermic = breaking bonds". Every reaction does both. Say instead: "the reaction is exothermic because more energy is released when bonds form than is absorbed when bonds break."

A reaction is exothermic. Which explanation, in terms of bonds, is correct?

  1. Only bonds are formed, none are broken
  2. The energy absorbed breaking bonds is greater than the energy released forming bonds
  3. The energy released forming bonds is greater than the energy absorbed breaking bonds
  4. Bond breaking releases energy and bond forming absorbs energy

Both processes always happen. Bond breaking always absorbs energy and bond forming always releases it; exothermic means the release is the bigger of the two.

Everyday examples to quote

Exothermic (ΔH < 0)Endothermic (ΔH > 0)
Combustion of fuels; respiration; neutralization; most polymerizations; the thermite reaction; corrosion (rusting, an oxidation); dissolving concentrated acid in water; anhydrous CuSO4 + water; nuclear fission (a nuclear, not chemical, process)Photosynthesis; thermal decomposition (e.g. of metal carbonates); dissolving NH4NO3 or KCl in water; Ba(OH)2·8H2O + NH4Cl or NH4SCN; ethanoic acid + sodium carbonate; dehydrating CuSO4·5H2O

Changes of state follow the same logic. Melting, boiling and sublimation need energy to overcome the forces between particles, so they are endothermic. Freezing, condensing and deposition release energy, so they are exothermic. (Ice does not "cool" your drink so much as your drink heats the ice: energy flows from the drink into the melting ice.)

Which change of state is exothermic?

  1. CO2(s) → CO2(g)
  2. H2O(l) → H2O(g)
  3. NH3(g) → NH3(l)
  4. Fe(s) → Fe(l)

Condensation brings particles closer together and forms intermolecular attractions, so energy is released. Sublimation, boiling and melting all need energy.

Reversible reactions

If a reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic by exactly the same amount in the other. CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l) → CuSO4·5H2O(s) is exothermic: add water to the white anhydrous powder and it turns blue and gets hot. Heating the blue crystals to drive the water off is endothermic. A reaction cannot be exothermic in both directions: that would create energy from nothing.

Exam tipIn equilibrium questions, "heating shifts the equilibrium to the right" means the forward reaction is endothermic. Raising the temperature always favours the endothermic direction.

Quick-fire: exothermic or endothermic?

The starting temperature of a reaction mixture is 20 °C and the final temperature is 25 °C. The reaction is…

  1. exothermic, ΔH negative
  2. exothermic, ΔH positive
  3. endothermic, ΔH negative
  4. endothermic, ΔH positive

The surroundings (the solution) warmed up, so heat left the system: exothermic, and ΔH is negative from the system's point of view.

Dilute sulfuric acid has an initial temperature of 24.0 °C and reaches a final temperature of 31.5 °C during a reaction. Calculate the temperature change, ΔT.

ΔT = final − initial = 31.5 − 24.0 = 7.5 °C, which is the same as 7.5 K. The temperature rose, so the reaction is exothermic.

A metal carbonate takes in energy from the surroundings to break down. What type of reaction is this, and what is the sign of ΔH?

Thermal decomposition that takes in energy is endothermic, so ΔH is positive. For example CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g), ΔH = +178 kJ mol−1.

title: Energy profiles and stability
html:
R1.1.3 Energy profiles and stability

An energy profile (reaction profile, potential energy diagram) shows how the potential energy (enthalpy) of the chemicals changes as reactants turn into products. It shows the enthalpy of the reactants and products, the activation energy Ea (the minimum energy needed to react) and ΔH.

Start with the simplest version: an energy level diagram with just two levels.

Activation energy

Even a reaction that releases lots of energy, like a burning match, needs an energy input to get started: striking the match. All reactions need energy to start them; otherwise fuels would burst into flame as soon as they met air. This energy barrier is the activation energy, Ea: the minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to take place. On a profile, it appears as the "hump". The top of the hump is the transition state (activated complex), where old bonds are partly broken and new ones are partly formed.

Reading the diagrams:

  • Exothermic: products sit below reactants. Products are lower in energy and so more stable.
  • Endothermic: products sit above reactants and are less stable.

"Stable" here means energetically stable: lower enthalpy. A system tends to move towards lower energy, which is why so many spontaneous changes are exothermic (R1.4 explains why this is not the whole story).

Exam tipExam marks usually go for: axes labelled potential energy / enthalpy and reaction coordinate / progress of reaction (never "time"); Ea as an upward arrow from the reactant level to the peak; ΔH as an arrow from reactants to products. A catalyst gives a lower hump with the same start and end levels, so ΔH is unchanged.

Practise reading profiles

What do A and B represent, and how does the diagram show the reaction is exothermic?

A is the activation energy. B is the overall energy change (ΔH). The diagram shows the reaction is exothermic because the energy of the products is lower than the energy of the reactants.

An exothermic profile is labelled with "1370 kJ" on an arrow from the reactant level up to the top of the curve. What does 1370 kJ represent?

  1. Activation energy
  2. Energy of the products
  3. Energy of the reactants
  4. Energy released

An arrow from the reactant level up to the peak is always the activation energy. The energy released would be an arrow from reactants down to products.

On an enthalpy profile the reactants are drawn higher than the products. What can be deduced?

  1. The reactants are less stable than the products and the reaction is exothermic
  2. The reactants are less stable than the products and the reaction is endothermic
  3. The reactants are more stable than the products and the reaction is exothermic
  4. The reactants are more stable than the products and the reaction is endothermic

Higher enthalpy means less stable. Going from high to low enthalpy releases energy, so ΔH is negative: exothermic.

On a potential energy profile the products are drawn higher than the reactants. Which describes the reaction?

  1. Endothermic, and the products have greater enthalpy than the reactants
  2. Endothermic, and the reactants have greater enthalpy than the products
  3. Exothermic, and the products have greater enthalpy than the reactants
  4. Exothermic, and the reactants have greater enthalpy than the products

Products above reactants means the system gained enthalpy: ΔH is positive and the reaction is endothermic.

title: Standard enthalpy changes
html:
R1.1.4 Standard enthalpy changes

Monitoring the temperature tells you whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic. But chemists usually need to know how much energy is transferred, and that depends on how much substance reacts, on the temperature and on the pressure. So we use a quantity called enthalpy, H: loosely, the total heat content of a system at constant pressure. We cannot measure H itself, only the change in enthalpy, ΔH, during a reaction.

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l) ΔH = −890 kJ mol−1

The negative sign tells you immediately that the combustion of methane is exothermic. "kJ mol−1" means per mole of reaction as written: here, per mole of CH4 burned.

The standard enthalpy change ΔH⦵ is the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions: 298.15 K (25 °C), 100 kPa, 1 mol dm−3 for solutions, with every substance in its standard state (its normal physical state under those conditions). The symbol ⦵ (a plimsoll or theta) indicates standard conditions. We need fixed conditions because temperature and pressure change the amount of energy given out or taken in, so values could not be compared otherwise.

Which set of conditions is used for standard enthalpy changes in IB Chemistry?

  1. 273 K and 101.3 kPa
  2. 298 K and 100 kPa
  3. 298 K and 1 atm only for gases
  4. 373 K and 100 kPa

298.15 K and 100 kPa (with 1 mol dm−3 solutions). 273 K is STP for gas volumes, a different idea.

Named standard enthalpy changes

Some enthalpy changes come up so often that they have names: enthalpy of neutralization, combustion, formation, vaporization and solution. Each definition is tied to one mole of something.

DefinitionStandard enthalpy of formation, ΔHf⦵: the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).
e.g. H2(g) + ½O2(g) → H2O(l) ΔHf⦵ = −286 kJ mol−1; 3/2H2(g) + ½N2(g) → NH3(g).
Most compounds have negative (exothermic) enthalpies of formation. ΔHf⦵ of an element in its standard state is zero.

Writing formation equations: one mole of product on the right; elements in their standard states on the left (diatomic gases as H2, N2, O2, Cl2; carbon as C(s), graphite); fractions are allowed and expected.

Write formation equations for KCl, CH4, CO2, MgO, CH3COOH, C6H6, C6H12O6, Al(NO3)3 and CuSO4, then reveal
  1. K(s) + ½Cl2(g) → KCl(s)
  2. C(s) + 2H2(g) → CH4(g)
  3. C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g)
  4. Mg(s) + ½O2(g) → MgO(s)
  5. 2C(s) + O2(g) + 2H2(g) → CH3COOH(l)
  6. 6C(s) + 3H2(g) → C6H6(l)
  7. 6C(s) + 3O2(g) + 6H2(g) → C6H12O6(s)
  8. Al(s) + 3/2N2(g) + 9/2O2(g) → Al(NO3)3(s)
  9. Cu(s) + S(s) + 2O2(g) → CuSO4(s)

Check: exactly one mole of product, and each element in its standard state.

DefinitionStandard enthalpy of combustion, ΔHc⦵: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance in its standard state burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions. Always negative (exothermic).
e.g. C8H18(l) + 12½O2(g) → 8CO2(g) + 9H2O(l) ΔHc⦵ = −5470 kJ mol−1 (data booklet).
Write combustion equations for Mg, CH4, C2H6, CH3CH2CH2OH, C6H6, C6H12O6 and H2, then reveal
  1. Mg(s) + ½O2(g) → MgO(s)
  2. CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)
  3. C2H6(g) + 7/2O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l)
  4. CH3CH2CH2OH(l) + 9/2O2(g) → 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(l)
  5. C6H6(l) + 15/2O2(g) → 6CO2(g) + 3H2O(l)
  6. C6H12O6(s) + 6O2(g) → 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(l)
  7. H2(g) + ½O2(g) → H2O(l)

Note: propan-1-ol contains one O atom already, so it needs 9/2 O2, not 5. Ethane is a gas. The combustion of H2 is the same equation as the formation of water.

DefinitionEnthalpy of neutralization, ΔHneut: the enthalpy change when an acid and a base react to form one mole of water. About −57 kJ mol−1 for any strong acid with any strong base, because the reaction is always H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l).

Which processes have a negative enthalpy change? I 2CH3OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 4H2O(l); II HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l); III H2O(g) → H2O(l)

  1. I and II only
  2. I and III only
  3. II and III only
  4. I, II and III

Combustion (I) and neutralization (II) are exothermic, and condensation (III) forms intermolecular attractions, releasing energy. All three are exothermic.

Enthalpy definitions to learn

Every enthalpy term used in the questions for R1.1 and R1.2. Learn the wording exactly: definition questions are usually marked on "one mole", "gaseous" and "standard states".

TermSymbolDefinitionExample / equation
Enthalpy changeΔHThe heat transferred between a closed system and its surroundings during a reaction at constant pressure. Negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic.kJ or kJ mol−1
Standard enthalpy changeΔH⦵The enthalpy change at constant pressure under standard conditions (298.15 K, 100 kPa, 1 mol dm−3 solutions) with all substances in their standard states.—
Exothermic reactionΔH < 0Heat is transferred from the system to the surroundings; the surroundings get warmer. Products have lower enthalpy and are more stable.CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O
Endothermic reactionΔH > 0Heat is absorbed by the system from the surroundings; the surroundings get colder. Products have higher enthalpy and are less stable.NH4NO3(s) → NH4+(aq) + NO3−(aq)
Activation energyEaThe minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to take place. Measured on an energy profile from the reactant level up to the peak.—
Specific heat capacitycThe heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g (or 1 kg) of a substance by 1 K. Water: 4.18 J g−1 K−1.q = mcΔT
Bond enthalpyBEThe energy needed to break one mole of a bond by homolytic fission in gaseous molecules under standard conditions. Always positive; data-booklet values are averages.H2(g) → 2H•(g), +436 kJ mol−1
Standard enthalpy of combustionΔHc⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance in its standard state burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions. Always negative.C4H10(g) + 13/2 O2(g) → 4CO2(g) + 5H2O(l)
Standard enthalpy of formationΔHf⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions. Zero for any element in its standard state.4C(s) + 5H2(g) → C4H10(g)
Enthalpy of neutralizationΔHneutThe enthalpy change when an acid and a base react to form one mole of water. About −57 kJ mol−1 for a strong acid and strong base; less exothermic for weak acids such as HCN.H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l)
Enthalpy of atomizationΔHat⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from an element in its standard state. Always positive. For a diatomic gas it equals ½ the bond enthalpy.Na(s) → Na(g); ½Cl2(g) → Cl(g)
Enthalpy of vaporizationΔHvapThe enthalpy change when one mole of a liquid turns into gas. Needed in Born–Haber cycles for Br2(l).Br2(l) → Br2(g)
Ionization energyIEThe enthalpy change when one mole of electrons is removed from one mole of gaseous atoms (first IE) or gaseous 1+ ions (second IE). Always positive.M(g) → M+(g) + e−
Electron affinityEAThe enthalpy change when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of gaseous atoms. Usually negative for the first electron affinity.X(g) + e− → X−(g)
Lattice enthalpyΔHlattice⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of a solid ionic compound is separated into its gaseous ions. In IB chemistry it is always positive (endothermic).MX(s) → M+(g) + X−(g)
Enthalpy of hydrationΔHhydThe enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to give a very dilute solution. Always negative.Na+(g) → Na+(aq)
Enthalpy of solutionΔHsolThe enthalpy change when one mole of a substance dissolves in water to give a very dilute solution. ΔHsol = ΔHlattice + ΣΔHhyd.NaBr(s) → Na+(aq) + Br−(aq)
Hess's law—The total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final states are the same.ΔHx = ΔHy + ΔHz

Enthalpies of neutralization, hydration and solution are not in the main textbook chapters, but questions use them, so they are included here.

title: Calorimetry, errors and uncertainty
html:
R1.1.4 Measuring enthalpy changes: calorimetry

How do you physically measure the energy taken in or released by a reaction? You let the reaction heat (or cool) a known mass of a substance whose heating behaviour you know, usually water, and measure its temperature change. Think of the burning fuel or food as "your reaction": the temperature change of the water is related to the energy it gives off.

The heat absorbed by the water is found from:

q = mcΔT ΔH = −q ÷ n
  • q is the heat transferred, in joules. It is not yet per mole; convert to kJ before finding ΔH.
  • m is the mass of the substance being heated (the water or solution, not the fuel). Take 1 cm3 of water or dilute solution as 1 g (density 1.00 g cm−3; be careful, not all liquids have this density).
  • c is the specific heat capacity: water 4.18 J g−1 K−1 (= 4.18 kJ kg−1 K−1). Rearranged, c = q ÷ mΔT, so its units are J g−1 K−1. The lower c is, the larger the temperature rise for the same heat.
  • ΔT is the temperature change of the water; a change of 1 °C is the same as a change of 1 K.
  • n is the moles of the limiting reactant. The minus sign makes ΔH negative when the water warms up.

The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 0.900 J g−1 K−1. What is the heat energy change, in J, when 10.0 g of aluminium is heated from 15.0 °C to 35.0 °C?

q = mcΔT = 10.0 × 0.900 × (35.0 − 15.0) = +180 J.

How much thermal energy is needed to raise the temperature of 25 kg of gold from 45 °C to 80 °C? (c for gold = 0.129 J g−1 K−1)

m = 25 kg = 25 000 g; ΔT = 35 K. q = 25 000 × 0.129 × 35 = 112 875 J (113 kJ). Always convert kg to g when c is per gram.

What mass of zinc (c = 0.3888 J g−1 K−1) requires 1000 J of thermal energy to raise its temperature from 50 °C to 60 °C?

m = q ÷ (cΔT) = 1000 ÷ (0.3888 × 10) = 257.2 g.

Combustion of a fuel

Burn a spirit burner under a known mass of water and weigh the burner before and after. Example: methanol, Δm = 0.348 g, 31.2 g water, ΔT = 30.0 K gives q = 31.2 × 4.18 × 30.0 = 3912 J = 3.91 kJ; n = 0.348 ÷ 32.05 = 0.01086 mol; ΔHc = −3.91 ÷ 0.01086 = −360 kJ mol−1. The data-booklet value (−726 kJ mol−1) is far more negative because of heat loss.

Worked example

A student burned 5.00 × 10−3 mol of pure butan-1-ol. The temperature of 175 g of water increased by 8.0 °C. Calculate ΔHc in kJ mol−1 (c = 4.18 J g−1 K−1).

  1. Pick out the data: m = 175 g, c = 4.18 J g−1 K−1, ΔT = 8.0 K.
  2. q = 175 × 4.18 × 8.0 = 5852 J = 5.852 kJ.
  3. ΔH = −q ÷ n = −5.852 ÷ 5.00 × 10−3 = −1170 kJ mol−1 (−1.2 × 103 to 2 s.f.).

Do not forget the negative sign: the water warmed up, so the reaction is exothermic.

Use the data in the figure to calculate the enthalpy of combustion of methylbenzene, C7H8, in kJ mol−1.

q = 250 × 4.18 × 60 = 62 700 J = 62.7 kJ.
M(C7H8) = 7(12.01) + 8(1.01) = 92.15 g mol−1; n = 2.5 ÷ 92.15 = 0.0271 mol.
ΔHc = −62.7 ÷ 0.0271 = −2.31 × 103 kJ mol−1 (data booklet: −3910 kJ mol−1, so a lot of heat was lost).

Bomb calorimeter: the fuel burns in pure oxygen inside a sealed steel container surrounded by water. Heat loss is much smaller and combustion is complete, so results are far closer to data-booklet values than a spirit burner and copper can.

Enthalpy changes in solution

Reactions in solution are easier: mix the reactants in an insulated container and measure the temperature change of the mixture itself. We still use q = mcΔT, where m is the mass of the whole solution and c is the specific heat capacity of the solvent (water). A nested polystyrene cup with a lid is a good, cheap calorimeter because polystyrene is a good insulator; it is only suitable for reactions in solution.

Worked example (textbook): Zn powder (1.37 g) and 28.8 g of 1.0 mol dm−3 CuSO4 give ΔT = 39.0 °C. q = 28.8 × 4.18 × 39.0 = 4695 J = 4.69 kJ. n(Zn) = 1.37 ÷ 65.38 = 0.0210 mol, which is less than n(CuSO4) = 0.0288 mol, so Zn is limiting. ΔH = −4.695 ÷ 0.02095 = −224 kJ mol−1.

Worked example

Neutralization. 50.0 cm3 of 1.0 mol dm−3 NaOH is added to 50.0 cm3 of 1.0 mol dm−3 HCl. Temperature rises from 18.0 °C to 24.6 °C.

  1. m = 50.0 + 50.0 = 100 g (use the total volume of both solutions, 1 cm3 = 1 g).
  2. q = 100 × 4.18 × 6.6 = 2759 J = 2.76 kJ.
  3. n(H2O) = 1.0 × 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol.
  4. ΔH = −2.76 ÷ 0.0500 = −55.2 kJ mol−1 (literature: −57 kJ mol−1).
Worked example

Unequal amounts. 400.0 cm3 of 0.500 mol dm−3 HCl + 400.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm−3 KOH; ΔT = 3.20 °C.

n(HCl) = 0.200 mol, n(KOH) = 0.400 mol, so HCl is limiting and 0.200 mol water forms. q = 800.0 × 4.18 × 3.20 = 10 700 J. ΔH = −10.70 ÷ 0.200 = −53.5 kJ mol−1. Divide by the moles of the limiting reactant, never the excess one.

Working backwards from ΔH

Worked example

Methane burns and releases 2225 kJ. ΔHc = −890 kJ mol−1. How many moles burned? n = q ÷ |ΔH| = 2225 ÷ 890 = 2.50 mol. The same rearrangement (n = q ÷ ΔH, then M = m ÷ n) lets you identify an unknown substance from its mass and energy change.

Challenge: 30.0 g of a salt is formed from its elements, releasing 211 kJ. ΔHf⦵ = −411 kJ mol−1. Find Mr, identify the salt and write its formation equation.

The process releases energy, so it is exothermic. n = 211 ÷ 411 = 0.513 mol. M = 30.0 ÷ 0.513 = 58.5 g mol−1, which matches NaCl (22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44). Na(s) + ½Cl2(g) → NaCl(s).

Heat loss and the cooling curve

Heat is lost from the system as soon as its temperature rises above that of the surroundings, so the highest temperature you actually record is lower than the value a perfectly insulated system would reach. Heat loss to the surroundings is the main systematic error. It always makes ΔT, and so |ΔH|, smaller than the true value.

To correct for heat loss, take readings every 30 s or so for a few minutes before mixing and for several minutes after. Plot temperature against time and extrapolate the cooling line back to the moment of mixing to find the maximum temperature. For an endothermic reaction the same method is used with the warming-back line.

Assumptions and sources of error

The usual assumptions: all heat goes to the water, the calorimeter absorbs negligible heat, solutions have the same density and c as water, and combustion is complete. In combustion calorimetry the main sources of error are:

  • Heat lost to the air instead of the water (the biggest one).
  • Incomplete combustion: soot on the calorimeter base shows less energy was released.
  • Heat absorbed by the copper can or beaker is not included in q.
  • Evaporation of a volatile fuel (e.g. ethanol) from the wick after weighing: mass burned appears too large. Keep the cap on the burner.
  • Water forms as a gas, not H2O(l), so conditions are not standard.
Common mistakeA negative percentage error (e.g. −16% for octane) means the experimental value is numerically smaller than the literature value. Heat loss always makes |ΔH| too small, never too large.

Tools: uncertainty and error in enthalpy experiments

  • Accuracy: how close a result is to the accepted value. Precision: how closely independent repeated measurements agree; it depends only on random errors. Uncertainty: the range within which the true value is said to lie, written e.g. 44.0 ± 0.4.
  • Random errors vary unpredictably from one measurement to the next (reading a scale from a slightly different angle, air currents on a balance, estimating between graduations). They make results imprecise (scatter). Reduce them by repeating and averaging, or by using a more precise, named instrument, such as a digital thermometer or a balance with more decimal places. They can never be eliminated.
  • Systematic errors make results inaccurate, always in the same direction and by the same amount or proportion (an unzeroed balance, always reading the meniscus from above, a miscalibrated thermometer, instrument drift). In calorimetry the big one is heat loss. Reduce it by insulating, adding draught screens, or moving the flame closer to the calorimeter. Most systematic errors can be reduced.
% error = |experimental − accepted| ÷ accepted × 100

A thermometer reading is only as precise as its smallest division. If you read 25.6 °C on a thermometer graduated in 0.2 °C, write 25.6 ± 0.1 °C: ± 0.1 °C is the absolute uncertainty, and the percentage uncertainty is 0.1 ÷ 25.6 × 100 = 0.39%.

Propagating uncertainties. When values are added or subtracted, add the absolute uncertainties; ΔT from two readings of ±0.1 °C is ±0.2 °C (and from two readings of ±0.5 °C is ±1.0 °C). When values are multiplied or divided, add the percentage uncertainties. A ΔH found by subtracting two large, similar bond-enthalpy totals can carry a very large percentage uncertainty.

Initial temperature 18.0 ± 0.1 °C, final temperature 25.6 ± 0.1 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in ΔT.

ΔT = 25.6 − 18.0 = 7.6 °C. Subtracting, so add absolute uncertainties: ± 0.2 °C. Percentage = 0.2 ÷ 7.6 × 100 = 2.6%.

Worked example

Neutralization with ΔT = 6.6 ± 0.2 °C (3.03%), [NaOH] = 1.00 mol dm−3 ± 0.18% (from weighing 10.00 g on a 2 d.p. balance, ± 0.10%, and a 250 cm3 volumetric flask, ± 0.08%), 50.0 cm3 pipettes of ± 0.05 cm3 (± 0.10%).

  1. n(NaOH) = cV: 0.18 + 0.10 = 0.28%, so n = 0.0500 mol ± 0.28%.
  2. Volume of mixture = 50.0 + 50.0 = 100.0 ± 0.10 cm3 (absolute uncertainties add), so the mass of water is 100 g ± 0.10%.
  3. q = mcΔT: add percentage uncertainties: 0.10 + 3.03 = 3.13%. With c = 4.2 J g−1 K−1 (as in the class example, taken as exact) q = 2772 J ± 3.13%.
  4. ΔH = q ÷ n: add again: 3.13 + 0.28 = 3.41%.
  5. ΔH = −55.4 kJ mol−1 ± 3.41% = −55.4 ± 1.9 kJ mol−1.

The temperature reading dominates the uncertainty, so a more precise thermometer (or a larger ΔT, by using more concentrated solutions) would improve the result the most.

Which change would most reduce the percentage uncertainty in ΔH for this neutralization experiment?

  1. Using a 3 d.p. balance to weigh the NaOH
  2. Using a more precise thermometer or a larger temperature rise
  3. Using a burette instead of a pipette
  4. Repeating the calculation with c = 4.18

The 3.03% from ΔT is by far the largest contribution; the balance and glassware contribute only fractions of a percent.
